Evan — thanks for the clear list, and great to hear the eng team is ready. High-level guidance below, then a couple of notes specific to DataStream.

Quick summary:
- Marketplace (AWS/GCP/Azure): fastest path to start — procurement can complete purchase with a credit card or marketplace PO, billing handled by the cloud provider. Ideal for short POCs or low-dollar pilots.
- Direct contract (private offer / Redwood invoice): slower to set up (legal + SOW/private offer) but gives you invoice/PO compatibility, custom terms (data, indemnities), and predictable annual commitments — usually better for committed production purchases.

Tradeoffs to consider:
- Timing: marketplace can go live within 1–3 business days once procurement approves. Private offers / direct contracts typically take 5–15 business days depending on legal and whether we need a custom SOW.
- Invoicing: direct contracts provide Redwood invoices payable to Redwood; marketplace invoices come from AWS/Azure/GCP which some finance teams prefer because they consolidate cloud spend.
- Co-sell & discounts: co-sell incentives are still possible with private offers and sometimes with marketplace private offers (AWS private offers). However, standard marketplace purchases (public listing) may not qualify for the same ISV co-sell incentives until a private offer is created or partner enrollment is confirmed.

For DataStream specifically:
- If you want a simple POC to validate performance, buy via the AWS Marketplace listing and we can enable a trial subscription. That avoids contract/signature delays.
- If you plan to convert to a committed annual seat/license after the POC and need a Redwood invoice or specific SLAs, we recommend a private offer (Marketplace private offer or direct Redwood purchase) so procurement retains a single vendor invoice and you can negotiate payment terms.

Next steps I suggest:
1) If POC only: procurement purchases a short-term subscription on AWS Marketplace (we can send the SKU and guidance).
2) If you expect to sign a 12-mo commitment: procurement requests a private offer; we will coordinate with our partnerships team to route co-sell and confirm any rebates.

Looping in Karthik for the co-sell/private-offer operational details (he owns partner flows).

—Monica

Evan — a few operational details to help procurement decide (copied from partner playbook):

1) Marketplace public listing (fastest)
   - Purchase through AWS Marketplace UI or API.
   - Billing: invoice from AWS (consolidated cloud bill). Payment via existing AWS billing instrument.
   - Eligibility: immediate start; no partner enablement required. No guaranteed co-sell rebate by default.

2) Marketplace private offer (recommended when you need invoice/terms)
   - We create a private offer in AWS Marketplace tied to your account. This preserves marketplace purchase flow but the invoice can be set up as an AWS invoice or, in some workflows, redirected depending on your procurement setup.
   - Co-sell: private offers can be routed through the AWS Partner Network to surface co-sell opportunities; requires enrollment and a short enablement step on our side.
   - Timeline: typically 3–7 business days once we have purchase order and customer account IDs.

3) Direct Redwood contract / invoice
   - Redwood issues an invoice to DataStream. Supports custom payment terms, data residency clauses, and SSO provisioning timelines written into the SOW.
   - Co-sell: we can still register the opportunity with AWS for co-sell but the mechanics differ — sometimes AWS prefers private offers for co-sell incentives.
   - Timeline: 5–15 business days depending on redlines and DocuSign turnaround.

Checklist for Procurement (what we need to move quickly):
- Target account IDs (AWS account number)
- PO number and billing contact (for private offer or direct invoice)
- Any legal must-haves (PO required, tax forms)

I attached a short PDF that walks through private-offer steps and partner registration.
